                                             A LAZARD CORRESPONDENCE FOR POST-LIE RINGS AND
                                                              SKEW BRACES

                                                                                 S. TRAPPENIERS


                                                    Abstract. We develop a Lazard correspondence between post-Lie rings and
arXiv:2406.02475v3 [math.RA] 18 Oct 2024




                                                    skew braces that satisfy a natural completeness condition. This is done through
                                                    a thorough study of how the Lazard correspondence behaves on semi-direct
                                                    sums of Lie rings. In particular, for a prime p and k < p, we obtain a corre-
                                                    spondence between skew braces of order pk and left nilpotent post-Lie rings
                                                    of order pk on a nilpotent Lie ring. This therefore extends results by Smok-
                                                    tunowicz.




                                                                                1. Introduction
                                              In 1954, Lazard proved a correspondence between Lie rings and groups satisfying
                                           certain completeness and divisibility conditions [23]. This built upon earlier work
                                           by Malcev [24]. The nowadays better known version of the Lazard correspondence,
                                           although more restrictive than the original version, states that for pk a prime power,
                                           there is a bijective correspondence between nilpotent Lie rings of order pk and
                                           nilpotency class at most p − 1, and nilpotent groups of order pk of nilpotency class
                                           at most p − 1. In particular, one finds a correspondence between groups of order
                                           pk and nilpotent Lie rings of order pk for k < p. This has proved to be very useful
                                           in the classification of finite p-groups, see for example [27].
                                              Pre-Lie algebras, also called left-symmetric algebras, arose as early as in 1881
                                           in the work of Cayley [12], only to resurface again 80 years later in the works of
                                           Vinberg [41] and Koszul [22]. See [8] for a survey on pre-Lie algebras. One of
                                           the motivations to study pre-Lie algebras comes from geometry, as they appear
                                           naturally in the study of regular affine actions of Lie groups [21]. More recently,
                                           the notion of a post-Lie algebra was introduced in the works of Vallette [40], see also
                                           [16]. For R a commutative ring, a post-Lie R-algebra is a Lie R-algebra a, whose
                                           Lie bracket we denote by [−, −], together with an R-bilinear map ⊲ : a × a → a
                                           satisfying:
                                           (1.1)                        x ⊲ [y, z] = [x ⊲ y, z] + [y, x ⊲ z],
                                           (1.2)                        [x, y] ⊲ z = (x, y, z)⊲ − (y, x, z)⊲ ,
                                           with (x, y, z)⊲ := x ⊲ (y ⊲ z) − (x ⊲ y) ⊲ z. If a is abelian, then (a, ⊲) is a pre-Lie
                                           R-algebra. A post-Lie Z-algebra, respectively pre-Lie Z-algebra, is called a post-Lie
                                           ring, respectively a pre-Lie ring. For a post-Lie R-algebra (a, ⊲), define
                                           (1.3)                          {a, b} := [a, b] + a ⊲ b − b ⊲ a.
                                           It follows directly from (1.1) and (1.2) that this defines a second Lie R-algebra
                                           structure on the underlying R-algebra a. We will denote this Lie R-algebra by a◦ .
                                              Braces were introduced in 2006 by Rump [30, 31] in the study of the set-
                                           theoretical solutions to the Yang–Baxter equation. They were subsequently gener-
                                           alized by Guarnieri and Vendramin to skew braces [18]. A skew brace is a triple

                                              2020 Mathematics Subject Classification. 20N99, 17D25, 20F40.
                                              Key words and phrases. post-Lie ring, pre-Lie ring, brace, skew brace, left nilpotent, Lazard
                                           correspondence.
                                                                                          1
2                                   S. TRAPPENIERS


(A, ·, ◦) with A a set and (A, ·) and (A, ◦) group structures such that
                           a ◦ (b · c) = (a ◦ b) · a−1 · (a ◦ b),
holds for all a, b, c ∈ A. Here a−1 denotes the inverse of a in (A, ·). When (A, ·)
is abelian, then (A, ·, ◦) is called a brace. For braces, the notation (A, +, ◦) is also
common (in fact, this is also the case for skew braces, but to avoid any possible
confusion we will abstain from using + for a non-abelian group operation). Skew
braces are essentially the same as bijective 1-cocycles of groups or regular subgroups
of the holomorph of a group. In this sense, they were already being studied in a
geometric framework in the form of regular affine actions of Lie groups on vector
spaces [3, 26] long before they were formally introduced. Since pre-Lie algebras
played an important role there, some connection between skew braces and pre-Lie
rings is to be expected. This was indeed first stated by Rump [32] for R-braces.
Bachiller then used the Lazard correspondence to construct a counterexample of a
conjecture on braces [4], starting from a counterexample by Burde [7] to a question
by Milnor [26] (note that the first counterexample to Milnor’s question was given
earlier by Benoist [6]).
   Smoktunowicz proved that the construction of the group of flows, as defined
for pre-Lie algebras in [2], could be adapted to left nilpotent pre-Lie rings of prime
power order pk , with k +1 < p, in order to obtain braces [37] with the same additive
structure. Here, a post-Lie ring (a, ⊲) is left nilpotent if there exists some n such
that an = 0 where a1 = a and ai+1 is the subgroup of (a, +) generated by a ⊲ b
for a ∈ a, b ∈ ai , right nilpotency is defined analogously. Similarly, a skew brace
(A, ·, ◦) is left nilpotent if there exists some n such that An = 1, where A1 = A and
Ai+1 is the subgroup of (A, ·) generated by the elements a ∗ b = a−1 · (a ◦ b) · b−1
for all a ∈ A, b ∈ Ai , right nilpotency is defined analogously. Recall that a skew
brace of prime power order is always left nilpotent [13]. It is not immediately clear
whether Smoktunowicz’s construction is invertible, an inverse construction is given
only in the case of strongly nilpotent braces of order pk , with k + 1 < p, and with
strong nilpotency index at most p − 1. Here strong nilpotency is equivalent to
the structures being both left and right nilpotent [35]. This correspondence was
used to classify all strongly nilpotent braces of order p4 , for p > 55 , in [28] while
the non-strongly nilpotent ones of this order were classified earlier in [29]. In [34],
Shalev and Smoktunowicz give a construction that starts from a brace (A, +, ◦) of
order pk , with k + 1 < p, in order to obtain a pre-Lie ring with additive group
(A, +)/{a ∈ A | p2 a = 0}. Although the strong nilpotency condition is no longer
present, one can not hope that this yields a correspondence as a quotient by a
non-trivial subgroup is taken.
   Recently, Bai, Guo, Sheng and Tang showed how from a regular affine action of
a Lie group onto another Lie group, one obtains a post-Lie algebra through differ-
entiation [5] (note that, although not explicitly stated in this way, this construction
also appears in [9]). This extended the earlier techniques to obtain a pre-Lie alge-
bra in the case that the latter group is Rn . Conversely, also in [5] a construction
by formal integration was given to construct a skew brace starting from a post-Lie
algebra of characteristic 0 and with some completeness conditions.
   In Section 2 we recall the necessary information on the Lazard correspondence,
and some basic notions on post-Lie rings and skew braces. In Sections 3 and 4 we
introduce the notion of filtered post-Lie rings and filtered skew braces. For both
structures we define the property of being Lazard in a natural way. We construct
a natural filtration on any post-Lie ring or skew brace. As a consequence, we prove
that if (A, ·, ◦) is a left nilpotent skew brace and (A, ·) is a nilpotent group, then
also (A, ◦) is a nilpotent group; see Lemma 4.11 and Theorem 4.12. This result was
previously proved by Cedó, Smoktunowicz and Vendramin for finite skew braces
       A LAZARD CORRESPONDENCE FOR POST-LIE RINGS AND SKEW BRACES                     3


[13, Theorem 4.8]. The introduction of a new notion of nilpotency for skew braces,
coined L-nilpotency, is essential in our proof and also provides a natural upper
bound on the nilpotency class of (A, ◦) in this case.
   In Section 5 we first prove that the exponential and logarithmic maps give a
correspondence between certain derivations and automorphisms of Lazard Lie rings,
mimicking the geometric correspondence given by integration and differentiation.
We then prove the final correspondence between Lazard post-Lie rings and Lazard
skew braces, its most general formulation is given in Theorem 5.9 and the version for
finite structures in Theorem 5.12. A more restrictive version of this correspondence,
although arguably the most interesting for classification purposes, is the following.
Theorem 1.1. Let p be a prime and k < p. There is a bijective correspondence
between skew braces of size pk and left nilpotent post-Lie rings of size pk whose
underlying Lie ring is nilpotent. This correspondence restricts to braces of size pk
and left nilpotent pre-Lie rings of size pk .
    This correspondence is explicitly described in Propositions 5.7 and 5.8. In par-
ticular, the brace associated to a pre-Lie ring is precisely the one obtained by the
group of flows construction as in [37]. Therefore, Theorem 1.1 effectively extends
Smoktunowicz’s correspondence [37, Theorem 14] which imposed stronger nilpo-
tency conditions. This provides an affirmative answer to [37, Question 1] and [20,
Problem 20.92 b)]. When Proposition 5.7 is applied to post-Lie algebras over a
field of characteristic 0, one recovers the formal integration by Bai, Guo, Sheng and
Tang [5, Theorem 5.22] with less restrictive conditions.
    In [5, Section 5.2] the authors propose the problem of finding a suitable differen-
tiation and formal integration theory for finite skew braces and post-Lie rings. One
such approach is precisely the one using the exponential and the logarithmic map
as in Section 5. On the other hand, a technique used by Smoktunowicz in [36, 37]
could also be seen as an discrete differentiation. In Section 6 we motivate this and
we give an application to skew braces that extends a result of Smoktunowicz.

                                 2. Preliminaries
   We first recall the precise statement of the Lazard correspondence together with
some useful related results. Although we use slightly different terminology, all of
the statements regarding the Lazard correspondence follow from the treatment in
[19, 23].
   For a group G and P a set of prime numbers, G is P -divisible if for every element
g ∈ G and every n whose prime divisors are contained in P , there exists a unique
                                                               1
h ∈ G such that hn = g. This unique element is denoted g n . If G is an abelian
group and its group operation is denoted by +, then we use the notation n1 g.
   A filtered group is a group G with a filtration of normal subgroups
                              G = G0 ⊇ G1 ⊇ G2 ⊇ ...
such that [Gi , Gj ] ⊆ Gi+j . Any subgroup H of a filtered group G has a natural
filtration given by Hi = H ∩ Gi . We endow a filtered group with the topology with
base {gGi | g ∈ G, i ≥ 1}. A homomorphism of filtered groups f : G → H is a
group homomorphism such that f (Gi ) ⊆ Hi . A filtered group G is complete if it is
Hausdorff and complete as topological space. A Lazard group is a complete filtered
group G such that G0 = G1 and Gi is Pi -divisible for every i ≥ 1, where Pi is the
set of all primes less than or equal to i.
Example 2.1. On any group G one obtains a natural filtration by setting G0 =
G1 = G and Gi+1 = [G, Gi ] for i ≥ 1. If there exists some k such that Gk+1 = {1}
(meaning that G is nilpotent) then the induced topology is discrete hence complete.
4                                            S. TRAPPENIERS


If we moreover assume that G is a p-group for some prime k < p, then G is easily
seen to be a Lazard group since every p-group is Pi -divisible for i < p. However,
note that any Pp -divisible p-group is necessarily trivial.
    Similarly, a filtered Lie ring is a Lie ring a with a filtration of ideals
                                         a = a0 ⊇ a1 ⊇ a2 ⊇ ...
such that [ai , aj ] ⊆ ai+j for all i, j ≥ 1. A homomorphism of filtered Lie rings
f : a → b is a Lie ring homomorphism such that f (ai ) ⊆ bi . We endow a filtered
group with the topology with base {x + ai | x ∈ a, i ≥ 1}. A filtered Lie ring is
complete if its underlying additive group (with the same filtration) is complete. A
Lazard Lie ring is a Lie ring whose underlying additive group is Lazard.
Example 2.2. On any Lie ring a one obtains a natural filtration by setting a0 =
a1 = a and ai+1 = [a, ai ] for i ≥ 1. If there exists some k such that ak+1 = {1}
(meaning that a is nilpotent) then the induced topology is discrete hence complete.
If (a, +) is a p-group for k < p then a is Lazard.
   The benefit of working in a complete Lie ring a is that the Baker-Campbell-
Hausdorff (BCH) formula can be evaluated in any two elements. Recall that this
formula originates in Lie theory and its first terms are given by
                            1         1                       1
(2.1) BCH(x, y) = x+ y + [x, y]+ ([x, [x, y]]+ [y, [y, x]])− [y, [x, [x, y]]]+ . . . ,
                            2        12                       24
where higher terms are of order at least 5. The prime divisors of the denominator
of coefficients of order n only involve primes ≤ n, which indeed ensures that these
are well-defined in a. The element BCH(x, y), for x, y ∈ a, is then interpreted as
limk→∞ BCHk (x, y) where BCHk is obtained by truncating the formula at order k.
Note in particular that if x, y ∈ a commute, then BCH(x, y) = x + y. In particular,
BCH(x, −x) = 0 and BCH(x, x) = 2x.
    Similarly, in a Lazard group A, one can evaluate formal infinite products of
commutators as long as their order goes to infinity and as long as the fractional
powers involve only primes ≤ n for commutators of order n. Two examples of such
formulae are the first and second inverse BCH formula (see also [15], [19]), whose
first terms are
                                         1             1                    1                  1
(2.2)          P (g, h) = gh[g, h]− 2 [g, [g, h]] 12 [g, [g, [g, h]]]− 24 [h, [h, [g, h]]] 24 · · · ,
and
(2.3)
                              1             1                  1                  1                  1
  Q(g, h) = [g, h][g, [g, h]] 2 [h, [g, h]] 2 [g, [g, [g, h]]] 3 [h, [g, [g, h]]] 4 [h, [h, [g, h]]] 3 · · · ,
where in this case [g, h] is the group theoretic commutator ghg −1 h−1 and further
factors involve iterated brackets of order at least 5.
Theorem 2.3. Let a be a Lazard Lie ring, then Laz(a) := (a, BCH) is a Lazard
group with respect to the same filtration. If f : a → b is a homomorphism of Lazard
Lie rings, then f : Laz(a) → Laz(b) is a homomorphism of Lazard groups.
   Conversely, let A be a Lazard group. Then Laz−1 (A) := (A, +, [−, −]), where
a + b := P (a, b) and [a, b] := Q(a, b), is a Lazard Lie ring with respect to the
same filtration. This construction is also functorial. Laz and Laz−1 are inverse
constructions.
Corollary 2.4. Let a be a Lazard Lie ring, then the Lazard sub Lie rings of a and
Lazard subgroups of Laz(a) coincide. Also, Lazard ideals of a and Lazard normal
subgroups of Laz(a) coincide.
       A LAZARD CORRESPONDENCE FOR POST-LIE RINGS AND SKEW BRACES                      5


  A filtered ring R is a ring together with a descending filtration of ideals
                                 A0 ⊇ A1 ⊇ A2 ⊇ . . .
such that Ai Aj ⊆ Ai+j . A filtered ring R is Lazard if its underlying additive group
is Lazard. If on a Lazard ring we consider the commutator bracket, then we obtain
a Lazard Lie ring. Note that a Lazard ring is necessarily non-unital, but one can
adjoin a unit to obtain the Dorroh extension R′ = Z ⊕ R with filtration R0′ = R′ ,
Ri′ = {0} ⊕ Ri for i ≥ 1. Then the exponential
                               ∞                n
                              X    1 k         X    1 k
                    exp(a) =         a = lim          a ∈1+R
                                  k!      n→∞      k!
                               k=0              k=0
is well-defined for a ∈ R. Similarly, for any a ∈ 1 + R the logarithm
                     ∞                             n
                     X          1                 X          1
           log(a) =     (−1)k+1 (a − 1) = lim        (−1)k+1 (a − 1) ∈ R
                                k           n→∞              k
                    k=1                           k=1
is a well-defined element and exp and log are mutually inverse. Then the Baker-
Campbell-Hausdorff formula is obtained as BCH(a, b) = log(exp(a) exp(b)). Simi-
larly, P (g, h) = exp(log(g)+log(h)) and Q(g, h) = exp(log(g) log(h)−log(h) log(g))
where we evaluate P and Q in the Lazard group 1 + R. Explicitly we have the fol-
lowing result.
Proposition 2.5. Let a be a Lazard Lie ring embedding in a Lazard ring R. Then
exp(a) is a Lazard group for the filtration exp(a)i = exp(ai ) and exp : Laz(a) →
exp(a) is an isomorphism of Lazard groups.
   Let a be a filtered Lie ring. We define End(a) as the ring of endomorphisms of
the underlying additive group (a, +). We have a natural filtration on End(a) given
by
                            End(a)j = {f | f (ai ) ⊆ ai+j },
which makes End(a) into a filtered ring. If a is complete, then also End(a) is easily
seen to be complete. Let End(a)+ denote the filtered subring of End(a) consisting
of all elements in End(a)1 . If a is Lazard, then it follows directly that End(a)+ is
Lazard.
Remark 2.6. Note that although the difference between End(a)+ and End(a)1 is
subtle, we consider End(a)1 simply as an ideal of End(a) while End(a)+ is seen as
a filtered ring on its own. Throughout this paper we use a similar notation for any
filtered ring, group or Lie ring to indicate the filtered substructure consisting of all
elements contained in the second term in the filtration.
  For a a filtered Lie ring and a ∈ a, we denote by ada the adjoint map b 7→ [a, b].
Clearly, ad : a → End(a) : a 7→ ada is a homomorphism of filtered Lie rings, where
on End(a) we consider the commutator bracket.
Lemma 2.7. Let a be a Lazard Lie ring, then BCH(a, BCH(b, −a)) = exp(ada )(b)
for all a, b ∈ g.
   At last, we fix some notation and recall some important substructures of post-Lie
rings and skew braces.
   Let (a, ⊲) be a post-Lie ring and a ∈ a. We obtain a new Lie bracket on the
abelian group a by defining {a, b} := [a, b] + a ⊲ b − b ⊲ a. This Lie ring is denoted
by a◦ . We will denote left multiplication by a as La , so La (b) = a ⊲ b. Note that
(1.2) states precisely that a◦ → End(a) : a 7→ La is a Lie ring homomorphism.
Definition 2.8. Let (a, ⊲) be a post-Lie ring. A sub Lie ring I of (a, ⊲) is
     • a sub post-Lie ring if I is closed under the operation ⊲,
6                                    S. TRAPPENIERS


      • a left ideal if x ⊲ y ∈ I for all x ∈ a, y ∈ I,
      • a strong left ideal if it is a left ideal and it is an ideal of a,
      • an ideal if it is a strong left ideal and moreover I is an ideal of a◦ .
Example 2.9. Let (a, ⊲) be a post-Lie ring, then the fix
                       Fix(a) := {a ∈ a | b ⊲ a = 0 for all b ∈ a},
is a left ideal. The socle
                   Soc(a) := {a ∈ a | a ⊲ b = [a, b] = 0 for all b ∈ a},
and annihilator
              Ann(a) := {a ∈ a | a ⊲ b = b ⊲ a = [a, b] = 0 for all b ∈ a},
are ideals. For the latter statement, note that for a ∈ Soc(a) and b, c ∈ a, it follows
from (1.1) that 0 = b ⊲ [a, c] = [b ⊲ a, c] and from (1.2) that 0 = [a, b] ⊲ c = −(b ⊲ a) ⊲ c
hence b ⊲ a ∈ Soc(a). As {b, a} = b ⊲ a, Soc(a) and Ann(a) are ideals.
  Let (A, ·, ◦) be a skew brace. Then we define λa (b) := a−1 · (a ◦ b) and in this
way we obtain an action of (A, ◦) on (A, ·) by automorphisms
                             λ : (A, ◦) → Aut(A, ·) : a 7→ λa .
Note that the operation a ∗ b := a−1 · (a ◦ b) · b−1 can also be expressed as λa (b) · b−1 .
Definition 2.10. Let (A, ·, ◦) be a skew brace. A subgroup I of (A, ·) is
     • a sub skew brace if I is a subgroup of (A, ◦),
     • a left ideal if λa (b) ∈ I for all a ∈ A, b ∈ I,
     • a strong left ideal if I is a left ideal and also a normal subgroup of (A, ·),
     • an ideal if I is a strong left ideal and also a normal subgroup of (A, ◦).
Example 2.11. Let (A, ·, ◦) be a skew brace, then the fix
                    Fix(A) := {a ∈ A | b ◦ a = b + a for all b ∈ A},
is a left ideal of A. The socle
               Soc(A) := {a ∈ A | a ◦ b = a + b = b + a for all b ∈ A},
and the annihilator
           Ann(A) := {a ∈ A | b ◦ a = a ◦ b = a + b = b + a for all b ∈ A},
are ideals of A.

                             3. Filtered post-Lie rings
Definition 3.1. A filtered post-Lie ring is a post-Lie ring (a, ⊲) together with a
filtration ai , i ≥ 0, of the Lie ring a where each ai is a strong left ideal.
   Let a be a filtered Lie ring. We define Der(a) as the set of all derivations
of a contained in End(a), these form a sub Lie ring of End(a) under the usual
commutator Lie bracket. Thus they have a natural filtration Der(a)i = End(a)i ∩
Der(a). Let δ : g → Der(a) be a homomorphism of filtered Lie rings. We define the
semi-direct sum a ⊕δ g as the direct sum of the additive groups together with the
bracket
                   [(a, x), (b, y)] = ([a, b] + δx (b) − δy (a), [x, y]).
It is well-known that this makes a ⊕δ g into a Lie ring. The proof of the following
statement is straightforward; the fact that this is indeed a filtration follows directly
from the Jacobi identity.
       A LAZARD CORRESPONDENCE FOR POST-LIE RINGS AND SKEW BRACES                           7


Lemma 3.2. Let a, g be filtered Lie rings and δ : g → Der(a) a filtered Lie ring
homomorphism. Then a⊕δ g is a filtered Lie ring for the filtration (a⊕δ g)i = ai ⊕δ gi .
If moreover a and g are Lazard rings then a ⊕δ g is a Lazard ring.
   In particular, we will be interested in the semidirect sum aff(a) := a ⊕δ Der(a)
where δ = idDer(a) and its sub Lie ring aff(a)+ = a+ ⊕ Der(a)+ . If a is Lazard, then
so is Der(a)+ since it is closed in End(a), and therefore also aff(a)+ is Lazard.
Definition 3.3. Let a be a Lie ring, a sub Lie ring g of aff(a) is t-surjective,
respectively t-bijective if the projection pra : aff(a) → a to pra : g → a restricted to
g yields a surjective, respectively bijective, map from g to a.
Proposition 3.4. Let a be a filtered Lie ring. Then there is a bijective correspon-
dence between operations ⊲ : a × a → a making (a, ⊲) into a filtered post-Lie ring
and t-bijective sub Lie rings of aff(a).
Proof. This proof is a slight variation of the proof of [10, Proposition 2.12]. We
therefore only give a sketch of the correspondence.
   If (a, ⊲) is a filtered post-Lie ring then {(a, La ) | a ∈ a} is its associated t-bijective
sub Lie ring of aff(a), where La (b) = a ⊲ b. Since the filtration on a consists of left
ideals we find indeed that the maps La are contained in End(a).
   Conversely, if we are given a t-bijective sub Lie ring g of aff(a) then we define
a ⊲ b as La (b) where La is the unique endomorphism of a satisfying (a, La ) ∈ g. In
this way (a, ⊲) is a filtered post-Lie ring. Since the maps La respect the filtration
on a we find that ai is a left ideal for each i ≥ 0.                                        
  Recall that for every post-Lie ring (a, ⊲) we can define the Lie ring a◦ with the
same underlying additive structure as a and Lie bracket given by (1.3).
Corollary 3.5. Let (a, ⊲) be a filtered post-Lie ring. Then a◦ is a filtered Lie ring
for the filtration a◦i = {a ∈ ai | La ∈ Der(a)i }.
Proof. Let g be the associated t-bijective sub Lie ring of aff(a) as in Proposition 3.4.
Then it is easily verified that the bijection pra : g → a◦ is a Lie ring homomorphism.
By transferring the filtration from g onto a◦ the statement follows.                  
Definition 3.6. Let (a, ⊲) be a filtered post-Lie ring, then (a, ⊲) is Lazard if both
a and a◦ are Lazard Lie rings.
   We now construct a natural minimal filtration on a post-Lie ring (a, ⊲). Induc-
tively define L1 (a) as a and Li+1 (a) as the subgroup of (a, +) generated by all
elements of the form a ⊲ b and [a, b] where a ∈ A, b ∈ Li (A). One easily verifies
that Li (a) gives a descending filtration of strong left ideals (a, ⊲).
Lemma 3.7. Let (a, ⊲) be a post-Lie ring, then setting a0 = a and ai = Li (a) for
i ≥ 1 makes (ai , ⊲) into a filtered post-Lie ring.
Proof. It is straightforward to see that the ai form a descending chain of strong
left ideals. It remains to show that [Li (a), Lj (a)] ⊆ Li+j (a) for all i, j ≥ 1. Let
h = {La | a ∈ a} ≤ Der(a) and consider the semi-direct sum t = a ⊕δ h where
δ : h → Der(a) is the inclusion map. Then we find [(a, Lb ), (c, 0)] = ([a, c] + b ⊲ c).
It follows that [t, t] = L2 (a) × [h, h]. For a Lie ring g we introduce the following
notation for iterated commutators: γ 1 (g) = g and [γ i+1 (g) = [g, γ i (g)]. Then the
previous equality can be rewritten as γ 2 (t) = L2 (a) × γ 2 (h) and by induction one
finds γ i (t) = Li (a) × γ i (h). It is well-known that [γ i (t), γ j (t)] ⊆ γ i+j (t), so in
particular
       [Li (a), Lj (a)] × {0} = [Li (a) × {0}, Lj (a) × {0}] ⊆ Li+j (a) × γ i+j (h),
thus [Li (a), Lj (a)] ⊆ Li+j (a).                                                          
8                                   S. TRAPPENIERS


  The above constructed filtration naturally yields a notion of nilpotency, which
we coin L-nilpotency. Note that for pre-Lie rings this is the same as left nilpotency.
Definition 3.8. A post-Lie ring (a, ⊲) is L-nilpotent if Lk+1 (a) = 0 for some k ≥ 0.
The minimal such k, if it exists, is the L-nilpotency class of (a, ⊲).
Lemma 3.9. Let (a, ⊲) be a post-Lie ring. Then (a, ⊲) is L-nilpotent if and only if
(a, ⊲) is left nilpotent and a is a nilpotent Lie ring.
Proof. From the definition of Li (a) it is clear that if (a, ⊲) is L-nilpotent then it is
left nilpotent and a is a nilpotent Lie ring.
   Conversely, assume that (a, ⊲) is left nilpotent and a is a nilpotent Lie ring.
Let a = γ 1 (a) ⊇ ... ⊇ γ d (a) = {0} denote the lower central series of a and let c
be such that ac+1 = {0} (recall that this is the left derived series defined in the
introduction). Assume Li (a) ⊆ γ k (a) for some i, k ≥ 1, then [Li (a), a] ⊆ γ k+1 (a)
hence Li+1 (a) ⊆ (a ⊲ Li (a)) + γ k+1 (a). In particular,
                        Li+c (a) ⊆ ac+1 + γ k+1 (a) = γ k+1 (a).
We now conclude by induction that Lkc+1 (a) ⊆ γ k+1 (a) = 1.                           

Theorem 3.10. Let (a, ⊲) be an L-nilpotent post-Lie ring of class k. Then a◦ is
nilpotent of class at most k and the k-th term in the lower central series of a◦ is
contained in Ann(a).
Proof. Let (a, ⊲) be L-nilpotent of class k and consider it as a filtered post-Lie ring
with its canonical filtration. Then a◦k+1 ⊆ ak+1 = 0, so in particular a◦ is nilpotent
of class at most k. Also, since a◦k = ak ∩ {a ∈ a | La ∈ End(a)k } but End(a)k = 0
and clearly ak ∈ Z(a) ∩ Fix(a), the statement follows.                                

   We end this section by relating L-nilpotency to the notion of transitivity (also
called completeness) for pre-Lie algebras, as defined in [21]. Let F be a field of
characteristic 0 and (a, ⊲) be a finite dimensional pre-Lie F-algebra. Recall that
(a, ⊲) is transitive if for every a ∈ a, the map
                              ra : a → a : b 7→ b + a ⊲ b,
is a bijection. However, if a◦ is nilpotent, then this is equivalent to the left mul-
tiplication maps La being nilpotent for all a ∈ a [33, Proposition 2]. By Engel’s
theorem, this is equivalent with the existence of some n such that La1 · · · Lan = 0
for all a1 , . . . , an ∈ a. It follows that transitivity coincides with L-nilpotency, or
equivalently with the fact that its associated filtered pre-Lie ring is Lazard. Indeed,
the divisibility condition is trivially satisfied, as ak = 0 for some k ≥ 0, also a◦k = 0
and thus also the completeness follows for both a and a◦ . Note that the condition
that all La are nilpotent also appears in [9, Theorem 3.1].

                             4. Filtered skew braces
Definition 4.1. A filtered skew brace is a skew brace (A, ·, ◦) together with a
descending chain of strong left ideals Ai such that it is a filtration for (A, ·)
Definition 4.2. Let G be a filtered group. By Aut(G) we denote the filtered group
automorphisms of G and we define a filtration by
                  Aut(G)i = {f | f (g)g −1 ∈ Gi+j , for all g ∈ Gj }.
Lemma 4.3. Let G be a filtered group, then Aut(G) is a filtered group.
       A LAZARD CORRESPONDENCE FOR POST-LIE RINGS AND SKEW BRACES                         9


Proof. Consider the semidirect product T = G ⋊ Aut(G). We identify G and
Aut(G) with the subgroups G × {1} and {1} × Aut(G). Note that the subgroups
Gi are normal in T . By assumption, [Aut(G)i , [Aut(G)j , Gk ]] ⊆ Gi+j+k , so by
the Hall-Witt identity we find that [Gk , [Aut(G)i , Aut(G)j ]] ⊆ Gi+j+k and thus we
conclude that [Aut(G)i , Aut(G)j ] ⊆ Aut(G)i+j .                                   
Lemma 4.4. Let A, G be filtered groups and λ : G → Aut(A) a homomorphism
of filtered groups. Then the semidirect product A ⋊λ G is a filtered group for the
filtration (A ⋊λ G)i = Ai ⋊λ Gi is a filtered group.
Proof. Since we are working in a semi-direct product we find that
               [Ai ⋊λ Gi , Aj ⋊λ Gj ] = [Ai , Aj ][Ai , Gj ][Aj , Gi ][Gi , Gj ],
where we identitify A and G with the corresponding subgroup of A ⋊ G. Clearly
[Ai , Aj ] ⊆ Ai+j and [Gi , Gj ] ⊆ Gi+j . Since λ is a homomorphism of filtered group,
also [Ai , Gj ] ⊆ Ai+j and [Aj , Gi ] ⊆ Ai+j which concludes the proof.             
   Let A be a filtered group. We will particularly be interested in the holomorph
of A, which by definition is the semi-direct product Hol(A) := A ⋊ Aut(A).
Definition 4.5. Let A be a filtered group. A subgroup G ≤ Hol(A) is transitive,
respectively regular, if prG : H → G is surjective, respectively bijective.
   Note that if we consider the natural action of Hol(G) on G, i.e. (g, λ)·h = gλ(h),
then transitive subgroups of Hol(G) are precisely the ones such that the associated
action is transitive. Regular subgroups are precisely the ones that induces a regular
(or also called simply transitive) action.
Proposition 4.6. Let (A, ·) be a filtered group. There is a bijective correspondence
between group structures (A, ◦) making (A, ·, ◦) into a filtered skew brace and regular
subgroups of Hol(A, ·).
Proof. The proof is only a slight variation of the proof of [18, Theorem 4.2], therefore
we only give a sketch. Let (A, ◦) be a group operation such that (A, ·, ◦) is a filtered
skew brace. Define G = {(a, λa ) | a ∈ A} ≤ Hol(A) then G is a regular subgroup
of Hol(A). Note that Ai are strong left ideals so indeed λa respects this filtration
for all a ∈ A.
   Conversely, if G is a regular subgroup of Hol(A), we transfer the group structure
of G onto A with the help of the bijection prA : G → A (or equivalently a ◦ b =
a + λa (b) with λa the unique map such that (a, λa ) ∈ G) and we denote this new
group operation by ◦. Then (A, ·, ◦) becomes a skew brace and by assumption the
maps λa preserve the filtration Ai , hence the Ai are strong left ideals.             
Corollary 4.7. Let (A, ·, ◦) be a filtered skew brace. Then (A, ◦) with the filtration
(A, ◦)i = Ai ∩ {a ∈ A | λa ∈ Aut(A)i } is a filtered group.
Proof. Let (A, ·, ◦) be a filtered skew brace and let G be the associated regular
subgroup of Hol(A, ·) as in Proposition 4.6. Then Gi = G ∩ Hol(A, ·)i makes G
into a filtered group. Transferring this filtration of G onto (A, ◦) through the
isomorphism (A, ◦) → G : a 7→ (a, λa ) now yields the statement.               
   The notion of a Lazard skew brace is now the natural one.
Definition 4.8. Let (A, ·, ◦) be a filtered skew brace, then (A, ·, ◦) is Lazard if
both (A, ·) and (A, ◦) are Lazard groups.
   We now introduce a natural minimal filtration on skew braces. For (A, ·, ◦)
a skew brace, define inductively L1 (A) = A and Li+1 (A) the subgroup of (A, ·)
generated by all elements of the form a ∗ b := a−1 · (a ◦ b) · b−1 and a · b · a−1 · b−1 for
10                                   S. TRAPPENIERS


a ∈ A, b ∈ Li (A). Note that Li (A) is the left hand version of the series Rn (A, A)
as defined in [1]. By induction, one sees that the Li (A) form a descending chain
of strong left ideals of A. Also, note that if A is a brace, then Li (A) = Ai , so we
recover the left derived series.
Lemma 4.9. Let (A, ·, ◦) be a skew brace. Then setting A0 = A and Ai = Li (A)
for i ≥ 1 makes (A, ·, ◦) into a filtered skew brace.
Proof. The proof is almost word for word the same as Lemma 3.7. The only non-
trivial part of the statement is that [Li (A), Lj (A)] ⊆ Li+j (A) for all i, j ≥ 1. Let
                             H = {λa | a ∈ A} ≤ Aut(A, ·),
and consider the semi-direct product T = (A, ·) ⋊β H where β : H → Aut(A, ·)
is the inclusion map. Then we find [(a, λb ), (c, 1)] = ([a, c] + b ∗ c, 1). It follows
that [T, T ] = L2 (A) × [H, H]. For a group G we define its lower central series as
γ 1 (G) = G and [γ i+1 (G) = [g, γ i (G)]. Then the previous equality can be rewritten
as γ 2 (T ) = L2 (A) × γ 2 (H) and by induction one finds γ i (T ) = Li (A) × γ i (H). It
is well-known that [γ i (T ), γ j (T )] ⊆ γ i+j (T ), so in particular
      [Li (A), Lj (A)] × {0} = [Li (a) × {0}, Lj (a) × {0}] ⊆ Li+j (a) × γ i+j (h),
thus [Li (a), Lj (a)] ⊆ Li+j (a).                                                         
   The canonical filtration introduced above leads to a natural notion of L-nilpotency
of skew braces, which for braces coincides with left nilpotency.
Definition 4.10. A skew brace (A, ·, ◦) is L-nilpotent if there Lk+1 (A) = 1 for
some k ≥ 0. The minimal such k, if it exists, is the L-nilpotency class of A.
  The proof of the following two is completely analogous to those of Lemma 3.9
and Theorem 3.10.
Lemma 4.11. Let (A, ·, ◦) be a skew brace. Then A is L-nilpotent if and only if A
is left nilpotent and (A, ·) is a nilpotent group.
Theorem 4.12. Let (A, ·, ◦) be an L-nilpotent skew brace of class k. Then (A, ◦)
is nilpotent of class at most k and the k-th term in the lower central series of (A, ◦)
is contained in Ann(A).

     5. A correspondence between post-Lie rings and skew braces

Lemma 5.2. Let a be a Lazard Lie ring, then Aut(a) = Aut(Laz(a)) as filtered
groups.
Proof. We know by Theorem 2.3 that automorphisms of a and Laz(a) coincide. It
remains to verify that the filtrations coincide. Let x, y ∈ a such that x+y ∈ ai \ai+1 ,
then
                   [x, y] + ai+1 = [x, y] − [x + y, y] + ai+1 = ai+1 ,
hence x + y + ai+1 = BCH(x, y) + ai+1 and thus BCH(x, y) ∈ ai \ ai+1 . We conclude
that x + y ∈ ai if and only if BCH(x, y) ∈ ai . In particular, for Aut(a) and x ∈ ai
we find BCH(φ(x), −x) ∈ ai+j if and only if φ(x) − x ∈ ai+j . We conclude that
indeed Aut(a)i = Aut(Laz(a))i .                                                      
Proposition 5.3. Let a, g be Lazard Lie rings and δ : g → Der(a) a homomorphism
of filtered Lie rings. Then there is a unique filtered group isomorphism
                           γ : Laz(a ⊕δ g) → Laz(a) ⋊λ Laz(g),
such that γ(a, 0) = (a, 0) and γ(0, x) = (0, x), where λ : Laz(g) → Aut(Laz(a)) is
given by λx = exp(δx ).
Proof. Consider the split short exact sequence of Lazard Lie rings
                       0           a         a ⊕δ g          g          0.
The functoriality of Laz then yields a short exact sequence of Lazard groups

             1         Laz(a)            Laz(a ⊕δ g)             Laz(g)           1.
Together with Lemma 2.7 this proves the statement.                                         

find that γ does not affect the second component. Define V : a × g → a as pra γ,

Proposition 5.5. Let a be a Lazard Lie ring. Then γ yields a bijective corre-
spondence between Lazard sub Lie rings g of aff(a)+ and Lazard subgroups G of
Hol(Laz(a))+ . Moreover, pra : g → a is injective, respectively surjective, if and
only if pra : γ(g) → a is injective, respectively surjective.
Proof. The first part follows directly from Theorem 2.3 and Proposition 5.3.
   Assume that g is a Lazard sub Lie ring of aff(a) such that pra : g → a is not
injective. Then there exists some non-zero element (0, δ) ∈ g. But then clearly
γ(0, δ) = (0, exp(δ)) ∈ γ(g) and thus pra : γ(g) → A is not injective.
   Conversely, assume that there exist (a, λ), (a, λ′ ) ∈ γ(g) with λ 6= λ′ . Then
(a, λ)−1 (a, λ′ ) = (0, λ−1 λ′ ) ∈ γ(g). Hence γ −1 (0, λ−1 λ′ ) = (0, log(λ−1 λ′ )) ∈ g and
thus pra : g → a is not injective.
   Assume that pra : g → a is surjective. Since prA and γ are continuous, the set
pra γ(g) = V (g) is closed in a. Assume that there exists some a ∈ a \ V (g), then
there exists a d such that V (g) ∩ (a + ad ) 6= ∅ but X ∩ (a + ad+1 ) = ∅. Let (b, δ) ∈ g
such that V (b, δ) ∈ a + ad . By assumption there exists some δ ′ ∈ Der(a)+ such that
(−V (b, δ) + a, δ ′ ) ∈ g. Since −V (b, δ) + a ∈ ad , we have
             −V (b, δ) + a + ad+1 = V (−V (b, δ) + a, δ ′ ) + ad+1

Remark 5.6. Transitive subgroups of the holomorph of a finite group play an es-
sential role in the theory of Hopf–Galois structures, see for example [14, 25, 39].
One can prove that for any finite p-group A there exists a filtration of A such that
Hol(A)+ is a Sylow p-subgroup of the usual holomorph of A (just considered as a
group without a filtration). If |A| = pk for k < p, then such a filtration has length
at most p, so A is a Lazard group and so is any subgroup of Hol(A)+ . Hence in
such a case, it follows from Proposition 5.5 that we can classify all regular p-groups
of the holomorph of A up to conjugation by classifying the t-surjective sub Lie rings
of aff(Laz−1 (A))+ .
Proposition 5.7. Let (a, ⊲) be a Lazard post-Lie ring. Then
                               W : a → a : a 7→ V (a, La )
is a bijective map and S(a, ⊲) = (a, ·, ◦) with a·b = BCH(a, b), a◦b = a·exp(LΩ(a) )(b)
is a Lazard skew brace, where Ω := W −1 . Moreover, W : Laz(a◦ ) → (a, ◦) is an
isomorphism of filtered groups.
   If a is abelian, then
                                           ∞
                                          X    1 k−1
                               W (a) =           L    (a).
                                              k! a
                                           k=1

Proof. Let (a, ⊲) be a Lazard post-Lie ring and let g be the regular Lazard sub Lie
ring of aff(a)+ associated to (a, ⊲) as in Proposition 3.4. Then W is a bijection
since it is the composition of the bijections a → g : a 7→ (a, La ) and V : g → a,
recall that the latter is a bijection by Proposition 5.5. In the case that a is abelian,
the explicit formula of W follows from Lemma 5.4.
    By Proposition 5.5 we find that γ(g) is a regular Lazard subgroup of Hol(Laz(a))+ ,
thus we obtain a Lazard skew brace (a, ·, ◦) where (a, ·) = Laz(a). Also a ◦ b =
a · λa (b) where λa ∈ Aut(a) is uniquely determined by the fact that (a, λa ) ∈ γ(g).
Since γ(a) = {(W (a), exp(La )) | a ∈ a} we find λa = exp(LΩ(a) ).
    Also, W : Laz(a◦ ) → (a, ◦) is a group isomorphism because it is the composition
of the group homomorphisms Laz(a◦ ) → Laz(g) : a 7→ (a, La ), γ : Laz(g) → γ(g)
and pra : γ(g) → (a, ◦).                                                              
    Note that in the case that a is abelian, one obtains the group of flows as in [2]. It
is less trivial to see how the above construction is related to the formal integration
as described by Bai, Guo, Sheng and Tang in [5]. Let F be a field of characteristic
0. Then Bai, Guo, Sheng and Tang proved that to any connected complete post-Lie
F-algebra (a, ⊲) one can associate a skew brace (a, ·, ◦) where
                     a · b = BCH(a, b), a ◦ b = a · exp(LΩ′ (a) )(b).
We first note that in our terminology their notion of a connected complete post-Lie
F-algebra is a Lazard post-Lie F-algebra (a, ⊲) such that moreover ai ⊲ aj ⊆ ai+j , or
equivalently, such that a◦i = ai for all i ≥ 0. Note that under this extra assumption,
if ai = 0 for some i, then ai−1 is contained in the socle hence Soc(a, ⊲) 6= 0. In
[17, Section 3] an example is given of a left nilpotent pre-Lie R-algebra with trivial
socle, so it can be given a filtration which makes it a Lazard Lie R-algebra but not
a connected complete R-algebra in the sense of Bai, Guo, Sheng and Tang.
   We quickly recall their construction: Let (a, ⊲) be a connected complete post-Lie
F-algebra (a, ⊲) and consider the universal enveloping algebra U(a) together with
the filtration where U(a)0 = U(a) and U(a)i is the subspace generated by x1 · · · xn
       A LAZARD CORRESPONDENCE FOR POST-LIE RINGS AND SKEW BRACES                      15


where xj ∈ adj such that d1 +· · ·+dn = i. This makes U(a) into a filtered F-algebra.
On U(a) we define a new multiplication ⋆ which for a ∈ a, b ∈ U(a) is given by
a ⋆ b = ab + δa (b), where δa is the unique derivation of U(a) with δa (z) = a ⊲ z
for z ∈ a. In this way, (U(a), ⋆) becomes a filtered F-algebra (where we keep the
same filtration as before). This operation is then extended to the completion Û (a)
with respect to the filtration in order to obtain a complete F-algebra (Û(a), ⋆). For
a ∈ a, we define Ω′ (a) = log⋆ exp(a), where the exponential map with respect to
the usual multiplication in Û(a) is first applied, followed by the logaritmic map in
(Û(a), ⋆).
   Recall that a embeds into Û(a). One sees that ρ : aff(a) → End(Û (a)), given
by ρ(a,δ) (b) = ab + δ(b) is a homomorphism of filtered Lie F-algebras. Here we do
not distinguish between a derivation δ of a and its unique extension to a derivation
of Û(a). Clearly, a ⋆ b = ρ(a,La ) (b) for all a ∈ a and b ∈ Û(a), thus exp⋆ (a) =
exp(ρ(a,La ) )(1). Since derivations map 1 to 0, also
                       exp⋆ (a) = exp(ρ(a,La ) ) exp(ρ(0,−La ) )(1),
where exp⋆ denotes the exponential in (Û (a), ⋆). By Proposition 2.5 and the defi-
nition of W , we find
                     exp(ρ(a,La ) ) exp(ρ(0,−La ) ) = exp(ρ(W (a),0) ),
thus exp⋆ (a) = exp(W (a)). We conclude that Ω = Ω′ .
Proposition 5.8. Let (A, ·, ◦) be a Lazard skew brace. Then
                              Ω : A 7→ A : a 7→ U (a, λa ),
is a bijection and L(A, ·, ◦) = (Laz−1 (A, ·), ⊲) with a⊲b = log(λW (a) )(b), is a Lazard
Lie ring, where W := Ω−1 . Moreover, Ω : (A, ◦) → a◦ is an isomorphism of filtered
Lie rings, where (a, ⊲) = L(A, ·).
   If (A, ·) is abelian, then
                                 ∞
                                 X  1
                          Ω(a) =      (−1)k+1 (λa − id)k−1 (a).
                                    k
                                 k=2

Proof. Let (A, ·, ◦) be Lazard skew brace and let G be the associated regular Lazard
subgroup of Hol(A, ·)+ . Then Ω is a bijection since it is the composition of the
bijections A 7→ G : a 7→ (a, λa ) and U : G → A with U . The fact that U is
bijective, follows from Proposition 5.5.
   From Proposition 5.5 it also follows that γ −1 (G) is a Lazard sub Lie ring of
aff(Laz−1 (A, ·))+ , thus we obtain a Lazard post-Lie ring (Laz−1 (A, ·), ⊲). We find
a ⊲ b = La where La is uniquely determined by the fact that (a, La ) ∈ γ −1 (G).
Since γ −1 (G) = {(Ω(a), log(λa )) | a ∈ A} we find that La = log(λΩ−1 (a) ).
   Also, Ω is (A, ◦) → L(A, ·, ◦)◦ is an isomorphism of filtered Lie rings since it is
the composition of the isomorphisms (A, ◦) → G : a 7→ (a, λa ), γ 1 : G → γ −1 (G)
and prA : γ −1 (G) → Laz−1 (A, ·).                                                  
Theorem 5.9. The constructions in Proposition 5.7 and Proposition 5.8 are mu-
tually inverse and functorial. The map Ω associated to a Lazard post-Lie ring (a, ⊲)
coincides with the map Ω associated to S(a, ⊲).
   Lazard sub post-Lie rings of (a, ⊲) and Lazard sub skew braces of S(a, ⊲) coincide
and moreover, Lazard left ideals, Lazard strong left ideals and Lazard ideals of (a, ⊲)
and S(a, ⊲) coincide.
Proof. It is straightforward to verify that S and L are mutually inverse construc-
tions and that their associated maps Ω coincide. We prove the functoriality of S,
the proof for L is analogous. Let f : (a, ⊲) → (b, ⊲) be a homomorphism of Lazard
16                                 S. TRAPPENIERS


post-Lie rings and set (a, ·, ◦) = S(a, ⊲) and (b, ·, ◦) = S(b, ⊲). Let Wa and Wb
denote their respective maps W . Then by Theorem 2.3 f : (a, ·) → (b, ·) is a homo-
morhism of Lazard groups. As W is an isomorphism between Laz(a◦ ) and (a, ◦),
it is sufficient to proof f Wa = Wb f in order to conclude that f : (a, ◦) → (b, ◦) is a
group homomorphism. This equality follows direct from the fact that f La = Lf (a) f
for all a ∈ a.
    The equivalence of Lazard post-Lie rings and Lazard sub skew braces is a direct
corollary of Theorem 5.9. In particular, note that for b a Lazard sub post-Lie ring
of (a, ⊲) we have Wb (b) = Wa (b). In particular, Wa (b) = b.
    Clearly the Lazard sub Lie rings of a invariant under {Lx | x ∈ a} and the ones
invariant under {exp(Lx ) | x ∈ a} coincide, which yields the equivalence of Lazard
left ideals. Taking into account Theorem 2.3, the equivalence of Lazard strong left
ideals follows.
    Let b be a Lazard strong left ideal of (a, ⊲). As W : Laz(a◦ ) → (A, ◦) is a
group isomorphism, we find that b is an ideal of a◦ if and only if W (b) is a normal
subgroup of (A, ◦). Since W (b) = b, the equivalence of Lazard ideals of (a, ⊲) and
S(a, ⊲) follows.                                                                      

Remark 5.10. Recall that a skew brace (A, +, ◦) is square-free if a ∗ a = 0 for all
a ∈ A. Similarly, we say that a post-Lie ring (a, ⊲) is square-free if a ⊲ a = 0 for
all a ∈ a. Note that the property of being square-free is preserved by S and L and
W = Ω = id in this case. Therefore these classes behave particularly well under
the correspondence and eliminate most of the computations involved.
   The construction L coincides (under the necessary assumptions) with the geo-
metric construction in [5, Theorem 4.3] (or in [9, Section 3]). We shortly recall
this construction. Let (G, ·, ◦) be a skew brace such that (G, ·) and (G, ◦) are
Lie groups and the map a 7→ (a, λa ) is smooth. One defines a post-Lie structure
on g, the Lie algebra associated to (G, ·), by starting with the group homomor-
phism λ : G → Aut(G, ·) : a 7→ λa , which naturally yields a group homomor-
phism α : G → Aut(g) : a 7→ dλa . Subsequently, differentiation yields a map
dα : g → Der(g) and (g, ⊲′ ) is a post-Lie algebra where a ⊲′ b = (dα)a (b).
   Let (a, ·, ◦) = S(a, ⊲) for a finite dimensional Lazard Lie R-algebra (a, ⊲). Then
(a, ·) is a Lie group and its associated Lie algebra associated is isomorphic to a such
that under this identification, the exponential map a → (a, ·) is just the identity.
Thus, under this identification of (a, ·) and a we have λg = αg . Hence, b 7→ a ⊲′ b
is the differential of the map λ : a 7→ exp(LΩ(a) )(b). We first determine dΩ. Since
ΩW = id, it is sufficient to determine dW . By (5.2), we find dW = id hence also
dΩ = id. The differential of the map exp(L) : a → Aut(a) : a 7→ exp(La ) in a ∈ a is
                                         d
                       d(exp(L))(a) =           exp(Lta ) = La .
                                         dt t=0
We conclude that (dλ)a = La and thus a ⊲′ b = a ⊲ b.
Example 5.11. Let A be a Lazard ring and let La denote left multiplication by
a. Then A+ is a Lazard pre-Lie algebra for a ⊲ b = ab and it is well-known that the
associated group of flows is given by a ◦ b = a + ab + b. We can verify this directly:
clearly W (a) = exp(a) − 1, hence Ω(a) = log(1 + a). We now find
                     a ◦ b = a + exp(Llog(1+a) )(b) = a + ab + b.
Conversely, starting from the brace (A, +, ◦) we find Ω(a) = log(1 + a) and thus
W (a) = exp(a) − 1. we recover the original multiplication as
        a ⊲ b = log(λW (a) )(b) = log(L1+W (a) )(b) = a + log(Lexp(a) )(b) = ab.
       A LAZARD CORRESPONDENCE FOR POST-LIE RINGS AND SKEW BRACES                        17


Recall that this is precisely the classical correspondence between two-sided braces
and Jacobson radical rings [31].
Theorem 5.12. Let pn be a prime power and k < p. There is a bijective cor-
respondence between post-Lie rings of size pn and L-nilpotency class k, and skew
braces of size pn and L-nilpotency class k.
Proof. Let (a, ⊲) be a post-Lie ring of size pn and L-nilpotency class k. With its
canonical filtration (a, ⊲) is a Lazard post-Lie ring since both a and a◦ are p-groups
with ap = a◦p = {0}. By Theorem 5.9 we obtain a Lazard skew brace of size pn and
L-nilpotency class k,
   Conversely, let (A, ·, ◦) be a skew brace of size pn and L-nilpotency class k. Then
with its canonical filtration it becomes a Lazard skew brace since (A, ·) and (A, ◦)
are p-groups and Ap = (A, ◦)p = {1}. By Theorem 5.9 we obtain a Lazard post-Lie
ring of size pn and L-nilpotency class k.                                           
   We are now ready to prove Theorem 1.1.
Proof of Theorem 1.1. Recall that any skew brace of order pk is left nilpotent by
[13, Proposition 4.4]. Also, if a skew brace or post-Lie ring of order pk is L-nilpotent,
its L-nilpotency class clearly can not exceed k. The statement now follows from
Theorem 5.12, keeping in mind the characterisation of L-nilpotency in Lemmas 3.9
and 4.11.                                                                              
   Let (A, ·, ◦) be a skew brace and a ∈ A. For an integer n we denote the n-th
power of a in (A, ·) by an and its n-th power in (A, ◦) is denoted by a◦n . The
following result extends Proposition 15 and Lemma 17 of [38].
Proposition 5.13. Let (A, ·, ◦) be a Lazard skew brace and let n be an integer,
then {an | a ∈ A} = {a◦n | a ∈ A} and {a ∈ A | an = 1} = {a ∈ A | a◦n = 1}, and
these sets are Lazard ideals of (A, ·, ◦).
Proof. We prove the statement for the first set, the second part is analogous. Let
(a, ⊲) = L(A, ·, ◦). Then it is straightforward to see that na is a Lazard ideal of (a, ⊲),
hence it is also a Lazard ideal of (A, ·, ◦) by Theorem 5.9. Since (A, ·) = Laz(a),
we find na = {an | a ∈ A}. Also, as W : Laz(a◦ ) → (A, ◦) is a group isomorphism
we find W (na) = {a◦n | a ∈ A}, but since W maps any Lazard sub post-Lie ring
to itself, we conclude that {an | a ∈ A} = {a◦n | a ∈ A}.                                
Proposition 5.14. Let (a, ⊲) be a Lazard post-Lie ring. Then the fix of (a, ⊲) coin-
cides with that of S(a, ⊲), and similarly for the socle and annihilator. In particular,
if a is nilpotent, then (a, ⊲) is right nilpotent if and only if S(a, ⊲) is right nilpotent.
Proof. The first part of the statement follows from the fact that W (a) = a whenever
a ⊲ a = 0 or λa (a) = a, which in particular is the case when a is contained in the
fix or socle. The second part of the statement now follows from Lemmas 5.3 and
5.4 of [1] and the analogous statement for post-Lie rings.                        

            6. Formal differentiation through roots of unity
   Let n ≥ 1. Recall that a primitive n-th root of unity of a ring R is an element
ξ ∈ R such that ξ n = 1 and ξ k − 1 not a zero divisor for 1 ≤ k < n. It is well
known that the finite field of prime power order Fpn has a primitive pn − 1-th root
of unity. Also, Z/pn Z always contains a primitive p − 1-th root of unity.
   Let R be a commutative ring and let M, N be R-modules. We say that a map
f : M → N is a homogeneous polynomial of degree k if f (rm) = rk f (m) for all
r ∈ R, m ∈ M . A map f : M → N is polynomial of degree less than k if it can be
                      Pk−1
written as a sum f = i=0 fi where fi is a homogeneous polynomial of degree i.
18                                      S. TRAPPENIERS


Lemma 6.1. Let R be a ring and let M, N be R-modules. Let ξ ∈ R be a primitive
n-th root of unity where n is invertible in R and let f : M → N be a polynomial of
                                                           Pn−1
degree less than n, with homogeneous decomposition f = i=0 fi . Then
                                  n−1

                                      ξ f (ξ −j m) = fk (m)
                                n j=0
for all 0 ≤ k < n and m ∈ M .
Proof. Evaluating the formula yields

                  n j=0                n i=0 j=0

since n1    j=0 ξ      equals 0 if i 6= k and it equals 1 if i = k.                  
   For k = 1, it makes sense to see the above manipulation as taking the directional
derivative of f through m and subsequently evaluating at 0. Therefore, in the above
setting, it seems justified to introduce the notation

Proposition 6.2. Let pk be a prime power, ξ ∈ Z a primitive (p − 1)-th root of
unity modulo pk . Let (A, ·, ◦) be a filtered skew brace of order pk such that Ap = {1}

Proof. It is clear that (A, ·, ◦) with the given filtration is a Lazard skew brace.
By Theorem 5.9 we know that (A, ·, ◦) = S(a, ⊲) for some Lazard post-Lie ring
(a, ⊲). In particular, a has a natural structure of a Z/pk Z-module since |a| = pk .
Since W (ai ) = ai , it follows from Lemma 5.1 that the assumption on the filtration
translates to ai ⊲ aj ⊆ ai+j for all i, j ≥ 1.

   Note that a filtration as in Proposition 6.2 exists precisely if A{p} = {1} where

where a ∈ A{i} , b ∈ A{k+1−i} , 1 ≤ i ≤ k. For braces this is precisely the chain of
